claim: Streblospio benedicti has a developmental dimorphism with two distinct developmental morphs: obligately feeding planktotrophic (PP) larvae and non-feeding lecithotrophic (LL) larvae.
source: There are two distinct developmental morphs which differ in their egg size, embryological development time, larval ecology, and morphology. These are either obligately feeding planktotrophic (PP) larvae or non-feeding lecithotrophic (LL) larvae.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript text describing the study system.

claim: The two morphs of Streblospio benedicti differ in egg size, embryological development time, larval ecology, and morphology.
source: There are two distinct developmental morphs which differ in their egg size, embryological development time, larval ecology, and morphology.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript text.

claim: Adults of the two morphs are morphologically indistinguishable outside of some reproductive traits and occupy the same environmental niches.
source: Despite these developmental differences, as adults they are morphologically indistinguishable outside of some reproductive traits and occupy the same environmental niches.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript text.

claim: The larval traits in Streblospio benedicti are heritable, meaning the differences in development are genetic and not plastic.
source: The larval traits are heritable, meaning the differences in development are genetic and not plastic (Levin and Creed, 1986).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Crosses between the two morphs are viable with no obvious fitness effects.
source: Intriguingly, crosses between the morphs are viable with no obvious fitness effects, and these F1 offspring can have intermediate larval traits compared to the parentals (Levin and Creed, 1986; Zakas, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: F1 offspring from crosses between morphs can have intermediate larval traits compared to the parentals.
source: Intriguingly, crosses between the morphs are viable with no obvious fitness effects, and these F1 offspring can have intermediate larval traits compared to the parentals (Levin and Creed, 1986; Zakas, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The two morphs proceed through the same developmental stages despite starting from eggs of different sizes (8× volume difference).
source: Spiralian animals have a famously conserved pattern of embryological cleavage (reviewed in Lyons et al., 2012), so unsurprisingly we find the two morphs proceed through the same developmental stages despite starting from eggs of different sizes (8× volume difference).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript text and supported by citation to spiralian development patterns.

claim: LL embryos take longer to reach an equivalent larval stage compared to PP embryos.
source: Despite the similarity in embryo morphology, there are some notable differences between the two morphs: the absolute time between each stage is shifted such that the LL embryos take longer to reach an equivalent larval stage, which is expected as larger, more yolky cells can take longer to divide (McCAIN, 2008).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript text and supported by citation.

claim: PP larvae are obligately feeding and have feeding structures, while LL larvae are not obligately feeding.
source: At the swimming larval stage there are some notable morphological and behavioral differences (reviewed in Zakas, 2022, Figure 1), notably the PP larvae are obligately feeding and have feeding structures, while the LL are not.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript text and referenced in Figure 1.

claim: Only 36.2% of all expressed genes are significantly differentially expressed between PP and LL at any stage.
source: Only 36.2% of all expressed genes are significantly differentially expressed (DE) between PP and LL at any stage in this dataset.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the RNAseq analysis.

claim: Early in development over a third of DE genes are significantly different between the morphs, but these differences tend to be quite small in magnitude.
source: We find that early in development over a third of these DE genes are significantly different between the morphs, but these differences tend to be quite small in magnitude.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the RNAseq analysis.

claim: At gastrulation the number of significant genes decreases to less than 5% of the total DE genes, however these remaining expression differences are much larger in magnitude.
source: At gastrulation the number of significant genes decreases to less than 5% of the total DE genes, however these remaining expression differences are much larger in magnitude (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The two morphs are more functionally distinct during early development, likely because of the different metabolic requirements imposed by differences in maternal egg provisioning.
source: It appears that the two morphs are more functionally distinct during early development, likely because of the different metabolic requirements imposed on them by the differences in maternal egg provisioning (Moran and McAlister, 2009; Zakas, 2022; Harry and Zakas, 2023).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data supported by citations to previous work.

claim: 354 genes (45.9% of DE genes) are heteromorphic, where both PP and LL expression patterns matched the same cluster.
source: We identified 354 genes from our set of DE genes (45.9%) where both the PP and LL expression pattern matched the same cluster.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the clustering analysis.

claim: 224 genes (29% of DE genes) are heterochronic, switching expression profiles between PP and LL.
source: There are 224 heterochronic genes, which is 29% of DE genes.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the clustering analysis.

claim: Most genes that switch expression profiles between PP and LL do so between the most similar clusters.
source: We find that most genes that switch expression profiles between PP and LL do so between the most similar clusters, and thus are near the diagonal.
evidence: This is a result from the cluster switching analysis.

claim: Most heterochronies are minor changes in the timing of gene expression.
source: This shows that most heterochronies are minor changes in the timing of gene expression.
evidence: This is a result from the Pearson correlation analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Heterochronic genes that are expressed earlier in PP are functionally enriched for mesoderm specification, cell fate specification pathways, and several organogenesis pathways.
source: Gene ontology (GO) enrichment tests show heterochronic genes that are expressed earlier in PP are functionally enriched for mesoderm specification, cell fate specification pathways, and several organogenesis pathways (others include BMP signaling, mesoderm specification, intestinal epithelial cell differentiation, and gene silencing (see Supplementary file 1)).
evidence: This is a result from GO enrichment analysis.

claim: Heterochronic genes which are shifted earlier in LL are enriched for many metabolic functions.
source: Notably, heterochronic genes which are shifted earlier in LL are enriched for many metabolic functions.
evidence: This is a result from GO enrichment analysis.

claim: 195 genes (25.3% of DE genes) are morph-specific, only expressed in one morph.
source: Using this approach, we identify 195 genes (25.3% of DE genes) which are only expressed in one morph (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the DAFS analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: There are considerably more P-specific genes (150 genes in PP vs 45 genes in LL), which tend to be expressed in later developmental stages.
source: We find considerably more P-specific genes (150 genes in PP vs 45 genes in LL), which tend to be expressed in later developmental stages.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the morph-specific gene analysis.

claim: Heteromorphic changes in expression account for most gene expression differences.
source: Overall, we find that heteromorphic changes in expression accounts for most gene expression differences, which is expected as this is the smallest change in gene expression of the three categories.
evidence: This is a summary of the quantitative results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Morph-specific and heterochronic changes make up very similar proportions of the remaining differences.
source: Morph-specific and heterochronic changes make up very similar proportions of the remaining differences (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary of the quantitative results shown in Figure 7.

claim: While true heterochronies are common, they are not the main driver of gene expression differences in development.
source: This demonstrates that while true heterochronies are common, they are not the main driver of gene expression differences in development.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the quantitative results.

claim: F1 offspring typically closely resemble their mother's phenotype.
source: Cross of the two developmental morphs to produce F1 offspring, which can have a range of intermediate traits, but typically closely resemble their mother's phenotype (Zakas and Rockman, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: F1s have a general pattern of intermediate expression values but have more variability within replicates and clear cases of outliers.
source: F1s have a general pattern of intermediate expression values but have more variability within replicates and clear cases of outliers (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the F1 expression analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: F1 gene expression patterns are split between those matching the maternal and paternal gene expression pattern, with slightly more genes matching the paternal expression at each stage.
source: For genes that are DE between PP and LL samples, we find that F1 gene expression patterns are split between those matching the maternal and paternal gene expression pattern, with slightly more genes matching the paternal expression at each stage (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a result from the F1 expression analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Most genes (>8000 genes on average, out of 14,327 genes expressed) have extremely conserved expression patterns among PP, LL, and F1 embryos at each developmental stage.
source: We find that most genes (>8000 genes on average, out of 14,327 genes expressed) have extremely conserved expression patterns among PP, LL, and F1 embryos at each developmental stage.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the expression analysis.

claim: Very few morph-specific genes are expressed at a significant level in either F1s (between 0 [PP] and 3 [LL] genes), strongly suggesting negative regulation of expression that acts in trans for these genes.
source: Notably, very few morph-specific genes are expressed at a significant level in either F1s (between 0 [PP] and 3 [LL] genes), strongly suggesting negative regulation of expression that acts in trans for these genes.
evidence: This is a result from the F1 expression analysis with an inference about regulatory mechanism.

claim: The primary mode of regulatory change throughout development is trans-acting.
source: The primary mode of regulatory change throughout development is trans-acting (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a result from the regulatory architecture analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: No differences are caused by purely cis-acting regulatory modifications.
source: No differences are caused by purely cis-acting regulatory modifications, though we did find some cis+trans and cis-×-trans interactions.
evidence: This is a result from the regulatory architecture analysis.

claim: The number of genes with compensatory regulatory modifications increases sharply after gastrulation.
source: We found that the number of genes with compensatory regulatory modifications increases sharply after gastrulation, indicating that gene expression may be more tightly controlled past that point.
evidence: This is a result from the regulatory architecture analysis with an inference about gene regulation.

claim: Many significant differences in gene expression between the F1 morphs arise at early stages (ostensibly due to the presence of maternal transcripts inherited through the egg) and then drop sharply after gastrulation.
source: Tests for differential expression show that many significant differences in gene expression between the F1 morphs arise at early stages (ostensibly due to the presence of maternal transcripts inherited through the egg) and then drop sharply after gastrulation (Figure 10; Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from the parental effects analysis shown in Figure 10.

claim: Most parental effects are limited to early embryogenesis, which is consistent with expectations for maternal transcription degradation.
source: This indicates that while a few parental effects on gene expression may persist throughout development, most parental effects are limited to early embryogenesis, which is consistent with expectations for maternal transcription degradation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the parental effects results.

claim: LL offspring take longer to reach the same embryonic developmental stages as PP in absolute time, although the stages are similar, and morphological differences are not observed until later development.
source: LL offspring take longer to reach the same embryonic developmental stages as PP in absolute time, although the stages are similar, and morphological differences are not observed until later development.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript text.

claim: Evolutionarily, LL is the more derived developmental mode, which likely arose from a maternal increase in egg size followed by adaptive changes in the genome that increased LL fitness.
source: Evolutionarily, we expect that LL is the more derived developmental mode, which likely arose from a maternal increase in egg size followed by adaptive changes in the genome that increased LL fitness (reviewed in Zakas, 2022).
evidence: This is an evolutionary interpretation supported by citation to a review.

claim: The non-obligatory-feeding LL larvae have a delay in mesoderm formation and through-gut development.
source: The non-obligatory-feeding LL larvae have a delay in mesoderm formation and through-gut development (Pernet, 2003; Gibson et al., 2010) so we would expect a delay in LL for mesoderm and gut specification, which we do see in the GO terms for the genes expressed earlier in PP.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and confirmed by the current study's GO analysis.

claim: The pattern of differential expression over development – where numerous but small expression differences occur early followed by a few genes with large expression differences – is consistent with the importance of gastrulation to canalize development.
source: The pattern of differential expression we observe over development – where numerous but small expression differences occur early followed by a few genes with large expression differences (Figure 2C) – is consistent with the importance of gastrulation to canalize development.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in the context of developmental biology theory.

claim: Gastrulation is the 'phylotypic stage' at which different phyla are the most morphologically and molecularly similar to each other during their development.
source: Gastrulation is the 'phylotypic stage' at which different phyla are the most morphologically and molecularly similar to each other during their development (Slack et al., 1993; Duboule, 1994; Richardson, 1995; Irie and Kuratani, 2011; Irie and Kuratani, 2014; Macchietto et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Previous genetic and transcriptomic work suggests there is very little differentiation of the two morphs at the genomic level.
source: Morph-specific genes are of particular interest in S. benedicti as previous genetic and transcriptomic work suggests there is very little differentiation of the two morphs at the genomic level (Zakas et al., 2018; Zakas et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Incipient species that are early in their divergence have more genetic regulatory changes due to trans-acting factors.
source: We expect that incipient species that are early in their divergence have more genetic regulatory changes due to trans-acting factors; this is because trans-acting factors may be more pleiotropic and initiate numerous developmental changes parsimoniously.
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation stated in the manuscript.

claim: As species divergence time increases, cis-acting elements can arise and refine gene expression of individual genes.
source: As species divergence time increases, cis-acting elements can arise and refine gene expression of individual genes (Wittkopp et al., 2004; Coolon et al., 2014; Cartwright and Lott, 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The life-history differences in this early evolutionary divergence are driven by a few developmentally upstream trans-acting factors with pleiotropic effects.
source: This suggests the life-history differences we see in this early evolutionary divergence are driven by a few developmentally upstream trans-acting factors with pleiotropic effects.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the regulatory architecture results.

claim: Heterochronic and morph-specific genes contribute similarly to gene expression differentiation.
source: We quantify the relative contribution of heteromorphic, heterochronic, and morph-specific gene expression pattern modifications in the evolution of a developmental dimorphism. We find that heterochronic and morph-specific genes contribute similarly to gene expression differentiation.
evidence: This is a summary of the quantitative results.

claim: The regulatory architecture of differential expression is predominantly trans-acting modifications.
source: Additionally, we find that the regulatory architecture of differential expression is predominantly trans-acting modifications, supporting the hypothesis that early gene expression evolution occurs by few, highly pleiotropic trans-acting regulatory modifications.
evidence: This is a summary of the regulatory architecture results.

claim: Lab-reared Streblospio benedicti were originally sampled from Newark Bay Bayonne, New Jersey (PP), and Long Beach, California (LL).
source: We use lab-reared male and female S. benedicti originally sampled from Newark Bay Bayonne, New Jersey (PP), and Long Beach, California (LL).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Methods section.

claim: All experimental procedures and growth incubations were carried out at 20°C.
source: All experimental procedures and growth incubations are carried out at 20°C unless otherwise noted.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Methods section.

claim: LL clutch sizes are 10-40 embryos per clutch and PP clutch sizes are 100-400 embryos per clutch.
source: This is necessary as embryo number is limited (10–40 embryos per clutch for LL and 100–400 for PP) and 10–40 pooled embryos are required to produce sufficient input mRNA.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Methods section.

claim: Six developmental stages were selected to capture a broad scope of developmentally critical periods: 16 cells, blastula (64 cells), gastrula (124 cells), trochophore, swimming, and 1-week.
source: We selected six distinct time points that we confirmed with cell counts (nuclei) using Hoechst: 16 cells, blastula (64 cells), and gastrula (124 cells). Time to each development stage was averaged over at least four clutch observations. Later embryo and larval stages were identified by morphological differences (appearance of ciliated band trochophores and eye development). Six stages capture a broad scope of developmentally critical periods while having enough timing separation to be distinct (each embryonic time point was ~12 hr apart).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Methods section.

claim: The threshold for significant gene expression differences is an FDR-adjusted p-value of 0.05 or less, and an expression fold-change greater than twofold.
source: Throughout this study, the threshold for significant gene expression differences is an FDR-adjusted p-value of 0.05 or less, and an expression fold-change greater than twofold.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Methods section.

claim: The S. benedicti reference genome is a chromosome-level assembly with >99% of genes occurring in the first 11 chromosomal scaffolds.
source: The reference genome for S. benedicti is a chromosome-level assembly with >99% of genes occurring in the first 11 chromosomal scaffolds (Zakas et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Methods section and supported by citation.

claim: LL and PP mapping rates do not differ significantly (two-sided t-test; p=0.1118).
source: We find LL and PP mapping rates do not differ significantly (two-sided t-test; p=0.1118), nor do the F1 samples' mapping rates differ from any other group (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the mapping rate analysis.

claim: Samples which received fewer than 2 million total reads were excluded from further analyses.
source: Samples which received fewer than 2 million total reads were excluded from further analyses since our expected sequencing depth was between 20 and 40 million reads (six samples total).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Methods section.

claim: The fuzzifier coefficient (m) required by Mfuzz was estimated to be 1.71.
source: The fuzzifier coefficient (m) required by Mfuzz was estimated to be 1.71 by the function 'mestimate' (Futschik and Carlisle, 2005; Kumar and E Futschik, 2007).
evidence: This is stated directly in the Methods section.

claim: A threshold of r<0.85 was selected to filter genes which would be classified as switching clusters but are similar enough in their expression between the two morphs to be removed.
source: Based on the distribution, a threshold of r<0.85 was selected to filter genes which would be classified as switching clusters but are similar enough in their expression between the two morphs to be removed.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Methods section.

claim: This filter disqualified 38 genes from being classified as heterochronic.
source: This filter disqualified 38 genes.
evidence: This is stated directly in the Methods section.

claim: Most of the variance in total gene expression is due to developmental stage and morph (PC1).
source: Using the full dataset, the first two principal component analysis (PCA) show most of the variance in total gene expression is due to developmental stage and morph (PC1; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a result from the PCA analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Pre-gastrulation development is distinctly separated from post-gastrulation by the second principal component.
source: Notably, pre-gastrulation development is distinctly separated from post-gastrulation by the second principal component.
evidence: This is a result from the PCA analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Approximately half of the heteromorphic genes are assigned to clusters 2 and 5.
source: Approximately half of these are assigned to clusters 2 and 5.
evidence: This is a result from the clustering analysis.

claim: Cluster 2 shows a pattern of maternal transcript degradation with no subsequent zygotic expression and is likely to contain genes associated with embryogenesis that are shared by both morphs.
source: Cluster 2, which shows a pattern of maternal transcript degradation with no subsequent zygotic expression, is likely to contain genes associated with embryogenesis that are shared by both morphs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cluster 2 expression pattern.

claim: Cluster 5 shows a pattern of largely post-gastrulation zygotic gene expression and these genes are likely to be associated with shared larval features.
source: Cluster 5 shows a pattern of largely post-gastrulation zygotic gene expression. Based on this pattern, these genes are likely to be associated with shared larval features.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cluster 5 expression pattern.

claim: Chitin catabolic processes are overexpressed in PP at the swimming stage (when they grow swimming chaetae) and are lowly expressed in LL which do not make swimming chaetae.
source: Although there are some late-appearing heteromorphic genes that are associated with discrete larval differences: 'chitin catabolic processes', for example, are overexpressed in PP at the swimming stage (when they grow swimming chaetae) and are lowly expressed in LL which do not make swimming chaetae (see Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a result from the GO enrichment analysis.

claim: The trend is early expression in PP genes compared to LL for genes with opposite expression profiles.
source: But where we see opposite profiles, the trend is early expression in PP genes compared to LL (top left corner).
evidence: This is a result from the cluster switching analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Many genes are expressed earlier in LL compared to PP but most of these are relatively small shifts.
source: That said, many genes are expressed earlier in LL compared to PP (bottom right orange triangle in Figure 5A) but most of these are relatively small shifts.
evidence: This is a result from the cluster switching analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There is a left-tailed distribution indicating that a few genes have a large difference in expression patterns (like a profile inversion) between PP and LL.
source: There is a left-tailed distribution indicating that a few genes have a large difference in expression patterns (like a profile inversion) between PP and LL (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a result from the Pearson correlation analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The shift in expression of metabolic genes is consistent with the life-history and feeding differences between the larvae.
source: The shift in expression of metabolic genes is consistent with the life-history and feeding differences between the larvae, and it may be that most of what is differentiating a PP and LL larvae is the onset of feeding and gut-related developmental programs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the GO enrichment results.

claim: Morph-specific genes include genes which code for proteins such as Fibropellin, Forkhead-box, Crumbs-like, Notch-2, and many zinc-finger proteins.
source: These include genes which code for proteins such as Fibropellin, Forkhead-box, Crumbs-like, Notch-2, and many zinc-finger proteins.
evidence: This is a result from the morph-specific gene analysis.

claim: GO enrichment tests for morph-specific genes expressed in PP found a few functions related to cell fate specification and signaling pathways.
source: GO enrichment tests for morph-specific genes expressed in PP found a few functions related to cell fate specification and signaling pathways (GO enrichment tests for biological process, p<0.05; no significant functional enrichments for LL-specific genes), but a distinct lack of genes involved in metabolic processes.
evidence: This is a result from the GO enrichment analysis.

claim: No significant functional enrichments were found for LL-specific genes.
source: GO enrichment tests for morph-specific genes expressed in PP found a few functions related to cell fate specification and signaling pathways (GO enrichment tests for biological process, p<0.05; no significant functional enrichments for LL-specific genes), but a distinct lack of genes involved in metabolic processes.
evidence: This is a result from the GO enrichment analysis.

claim: Metabolic pathways genes shifted earlier in the development of LL offspring are still required in both offspring morphs.
source: This is because metabolic pathways genes shifted earlier in the development of LL offspring are still required in both offspring morphs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the GO enrichment results.

claim: PP embryos require a few specific cell types to produce a PP larval form that are reduced or lost in LL.
source: These findings also imply that PP embryos require a few specific cell types to produce a PP larval form that are reduced or lost in LL.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the morph-specific gene results.

claim: F1s have considerably more variability across replicates, and some genes are misexpressed.
source: F1s have a general pattern of intermediate expression values but have more variability within replicates and clear cases of outliers (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1). They have considerably more variability across replicates, and some genes are misexpressed – where the F1 expression value is outside the range of the parental difference (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a result from the F1 expression analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Misexpression is reported in hybridization studies and is thought to be the result of epistatic interactions between divergent genomes that reduce the fitness of offspring contributing to sympatric speciation.
source: Misexpression is reported in hybridization studies and is thought to be the result of epistatic interactions between divergent genomes that reduce the fitness of offspring contributing to sympatric speciation (Norrström et al., 2011; Moran et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Whether misexpression affects the fitness of the embryos in S. benedicti is unclear, although F1s typically develop normally in the lab and no systematic reduction in viability has been observed.
source: Whether misexpression affects the fitness of the embryos in S. benedicti is unclear, although F1s typically develop normally in the lab and no systematic reduction in viability has been observed.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: In previous studies of gene expression in eggs of the two morphs, F1 eggs typically have intermediate expression values compared to parental genotypes, but high levels of misexpression.
source: In previous studies of gene expression in eggs of the two morphs, we saw a similar pattern where F1 eggs typically have intermediate expression values compared to parental genotypes, but high levels of misexpression (Harry and Zakas, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The high proportion of genes matching paternal expression patterns in early development is somewhat unexpected given that most transcripts in the first and second stages of development are expected to be maternally derived.
source: We expect most transcripts in the first and second stages of development to be maternally derived, so the high proportion of genes matching paternal expression patterns is somewhat unexpected.
evidence: This is an observation that contradicts expectations.

claim: The high variability and misexpression of F1s negatively impacts statistical power by introducing variation and results in fewer genes being confidently assigned gene regulatory mechanisms.
source: The high variability and misexpression of F1s negatively impacts our statistical power by introducing variation and results in fewer genes being confidently assigned gene regulatory mechanisms.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the F1 results.

claim: Almost no genes can be identified as having a dominant or additive inheritance pattern, while 150 genes are identified as overdominant over the course of development.
source: As a result, almost no genes can be identified as having a dominant or additive inheritance pattern, while 150 genes are identified as overdominant over the course of development.
evidence: This is a result from the mode of inheritance analysis.

claim: Not all genes have alleles that can be assigned parentage in the intraspecific comparison due to little fixed genomic differences between the morphs.
source: As this is an intraspecific comparison with little fixed genomic differences between the morphs, not all genes have alleles that can be assigned parentage; however, a set of ~2000 DE genes have morph-differentiating SNPs enabling the parental assignment of F1 transcript reads.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript text.

claim: A set of ~2000 DE genes have morph-differentiating SNPs enabling the parental assignment of F1 transcript reads.
source: As this is an intraspecific comparison with little fixed genomic differences between the morphs, not all genes have alleles that can be assigned parentage; however, a set of ~2000 DE genes have morph-differentiating SNPs enabling the parental assignment of F1 transcript reads.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript text.

claim: Only 143 genes have informative regulatory mode assignments due to misexpression in F1 offspring causing many genes to receive ambiguous assignments.
source: Of this set, misexpression in F1 offspring causes many genes to receive ambiguous assignments. As a result, only 143 genes have informative regulatory mode assignments.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript text.

claim: The genes that can be classified for regulatory mode are expected to be proportionally representative of the remaining regulatory architecture.
source: While this is a small number, we expect that the genes we can classify are proportionally representative of the remaining regulatory architecture.
evidence: This is an assumption stated in the manuscript.

claim: Studies across Drosophila species have indicated that maternal effects are regulated differently than zygotic effects.
source: Studies across Drosophila species, for example, have indicated that maternal effects are regulated differently than zygotic effects, but in this case there are larger trans-acting factors in early (maternally controlled) developmental stages (Cartwright and Lott, 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Comparison across the egg (maternal) and embryo (maternal and zygotic) regulatory landscape shows greater cis-acting regulation in the maternally expressed genes.
source: Comparison across the egg (maternal) and embryo (maternal and zygotic) regulatory landscape shows greater cis-acting regulation in the maternally expressed genes.
evidence: This is a result from comparing the current study to previous work.

claim: Maternal and zygotic gene regulatory architecture may evolve through distinct mechanisms and on separate timescales.
source: These results demonstrate the possibility that maternal and zygotic gene regulatory architecture evolve through distinct mechanisms and on separate timescales.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the regulatory architecture results.

claim: Splitting analyses into separate PL and LP parental arrangements did not yield significantly different results for regulatory mode changes.
source: We tested the possibility that the reciprocal F1s generated in the study (for the three stages that have both LP and PL samples) might have different regulatory mode changes due to parental effects. Splitting our analyses into separate PL and LP parental arrangements did not yield significantly different results, but treating them separately meant fewer genes could be assigned a mode.
evidence: This is a result from the regulatory mode analysis.

claim: Due to animal constraints where LL mothers produce far fewer offspring per clutch (10–40 on average), only three developmental stages were sampled for F1 offspring with L mothers (LP).
source: Due to animal constraints where LL mothers produce far fewer offspring per clutch (10–40 on average), we were only able to collect samples for F1 offspring with L mothers (LP) for three developmental stages (16-cell, gastrula, and swimming).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript text.

claim: All six time points were sampled for F1s with PP mothers (PL).
source: All six time points were sampled for F1s with PP mothers (PL).
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript text.

claim: Genes associated with feeding processes, growth, and cell cycle and specification are expected to initiate faster in the smaller, PP embryo.
source: For example, we may expect that genes associated with feeding processes, growth, and cell cycle and specification initiate faster in the smaller, PP embryo (Wray and Lowe, 2000; Strathmann, 2000; Lowe et al., 2002; Segers et al., 2012; Figueroa et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an expectation based on cited literature.

claim: The few genes that remain significantly DE post gastrulation are candidates for maintaining morphological and life-history differences between the morphs.
source: The few genes that remain significantly DE post gastrulation are candidates for maintaining morphological and life-history differences between the morphs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the differential expression results.

claim: Chitin biosynthesis genes remain significantly different at later stages, and are upregulated in PP.
source: (Chitin biosynthesis genes, for example, remain significantly different at later stages, and upregulated in PP.)
evidence: This is a result from the differential expression analysis.

claim: Gene expression levels might converge much later in development as both morphs reach adulthood.
source: However, these genes' expression levels might converge much later in development as both morphs reach adulthood.
evidence: This is speculation about later developmental stages.

claim: Given previous findings of limited total sequence differentiation between morphs, genomic rearrangements, gene duplications, or co-options underlying the expression of morph-specific genes are unlikely.
source: While it is possible that genomic rearrangements (Janssen et al., 2001), gene duplications (Long et al., 2003), or co-options (Linksvayer and Wade, 2005) underlie the expression of morph-specific genes, given previous findings of limited total sequence differentiation between morphs (Zakas et al., 2018; Zakas et al., 2022), we find these possibilities unlikely.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on previous findings and cited literature.
